security_controls.assessment: isAuthorized/denyAll/isAccounting are applied to baskets, complaints, privacy requests, B2B, 2FA and several generated API resources. Coverage is inconsistent: PUT /api/Products/:id authorization is commented out, /api/Deliverys, /rest/order-history, /rest/deluxe-membership, /rest/memories, /rest/chat and /rest/products/:id/reviews PUT show no authorization middleware in the inspected slices. The /api/Quantitys/:id IpFilter uses a placeholder address.

The coupon limit (max 10%) and eligibility conditions exist only in the system prompt. The generateCoupon tool accepts any number with no server-side cap, order validation or authentication, so model-directed action authorization depends on prompt compliance. getOrderById does check authentication and ownership (compared by vowel-masked email). The model-chosen searchProducts and getProductReviews tools have no per-user scoping. The /rest/chat route has no auth middleware, and the flow evidence says the token is decoded without signature verification. The system prompt also embeds a confidential discount instruction.
security_controls.control: Chatbot tool-level authorization and coupon policy

security_controls.assessment: Zod schemas give type checks. getProductReviews coerces the id with Number() before building a $where string, which limits injection to numeric values (NaN is still concatenated). searchProducts uses Sequelize Op.like with a parameterized value, but wildcard characters in the query are not escaped.
security_controls.control: Chatbot tool input validation and query construction

security_controls.assessment: The server fetches a requester-supplied URL with no scheme, host or private-range allowlist and no size limit. The response is written to disk under a user-id-based name with an extension that is allowlisted or defaults to jpg. Only a logged-in cookie session is required. On fetch failure the raw URL is stored as the profile image. No SSRF mitigation was found.
security_controls.domain: File Parser and Outbound Request Controls

security_controls.assessment: The memory upload applies a mime allowlist (client-declared type), sanitizeFilename and a timestamp suffix. The memory-upload multer is configured without a fileSize limit, while the memory-storage multer is limited to 200 KB. /file-upload adds size and type checks. Mime types are taken from the client header, not content.
security_controls.control: Upload handling (size, mime type, filename sanitization)
security_controls.domain: File Parser and Outbound Request Controls

security_controls.assessment: Rate limits apply only to reset-password and the 2FA endpoints. The reset-password key generator trusts the X-Forwarded-For header (spoofable, so the limit can be bypassed). The limit is 100 per 5 minutes, and validate:false is set on the 2FA limiters. The login, chat (LLM cost) and upload endpoints show no limiter.
security_controls.domain: Operations Runtime and Supply Chain Controls

security_controls.assessment: Rotating access logs (2 days retention) are written via morgan. However, /support/logs directory browsing with file serving and the unauthenticated /metrics endpoint expose operational data without authentication in the inspected code. Retention is short.
security_controls.domain: Operations Runtime and Supply Chain Controls

security_controls.assessment: cookie-parser uses a hardcoded static secret 'kekse' in source. Profile routes authenticate via an in-memory token map lookup using the cookie token. Request bodies of any content type are parsed as text and JSON.parse is applied without a try/catch, which can raise errors.
security_controls.control: Cookie signing and request body parsing

security_controls.assessment: Sequelize opens a file-based SQLite database at data/juiceshop.sqlite with placeholder credentials ('username'/'password') that SQLite ignores. No database-level authentication or encryption at rest is configured in this code. Protection depends on process and filesystem access controls, which were not inspected.

Transactions use IMMEDIATE mode, and SQLITE_BUSY errors are retried up to 5 times, which supports write integrity under contention. Sequelize query logging is disabled (logging: false), so this layer gives no data-access audit trail. Only models/index.ts was inspected, so model-level validation and setters were not assessed.
security_controls.control: Database query logging and transaction/retry handling

security_controls.assessment: Third-party actions in the inspected workflows (ci, release, zap_scan) are pinned to full commit SHAs with version comments, limiting tag-hijack supply-chain risk. One action (dawidd6/action-get-tag) is flagged as archived in a TODO but is still pinned and used in the release path. Other workflows were not inspected.

security_controls.assessment: Release jobs install global CLI tools (grunt-cli unpinned, typescript and cyclonedx with semver ranges) and use npm install rather than npm ci, so release artifacts are not built from locked dependency versions. The lint job uses --ignore-scripts, which is a good practice, but test and release installs run lifecycle scripts. A CycloneDX SBOM tool is part of the build.

security_controls.assessment: Registry and Slack credentials come from GitHub secrets, and the release is triggered only by version tags. No explicit top-level `permissions:` block was seen in the inspected files, so GITHUB_TOKEN scope depends on repository defaults. Releases are created as drafts, which adds a manual publication gate. Docker publishing has no visible provenance or signing step.

security_controls.assessment: walletNFTVerify trusts a client-supplied walletAddress from the request body and checks it against an in-memory set of minters populated from on-chain events. No signature or proof of key control is required, so any caller who knows a minter address can claim it. Entries are consumed on use, which limits replay of the same address.
security_controls.control: Wallet ownership verification for NFT mint challenge

security_controls.assessment: The handlers in the cited slices perform no authentication or authorization checks. Any caller can trigger creation of the shared WebSocket listeners. Handler-chain middleware outside these slices was not inspected beyond the flow metadata, which records no credential check.

req.body.walletAddress is added to an unbounded in-memory Set without any type, format or size validation. Unauthenticated callers can grow the set without limit, which is a memory-exhaustion risk, and can pre-register arbitrary addresses.

The Alchemy API key is read from the environment rather than hardcoded, and the connection uses wss. However, the key is embedded in the URL path and falls back to an empty string when unset. Provider errors are logged with error.message, which could expose the URL.

The JWT is stored in localStorage and in a script-set cookie. The cookie is set from JavaScript, so it cannot be HttpOnly. Any XSS can read the token. The cookie expiry is 8 hours. Failed login clears the stored token.

Google login uses response_type=token (implicit flow) with no state or nonce parameter and no PKCE. The access token is passed in a URL query string to the userinfo endpoint. A redirect URI allow-list from server configuration (lines 80-87) is a partial mitigation.

The client source contains hardcoded testing credentials. Password change sends the current and new passwords as GET query parameters, so they can appear in logs and history. Login validation only requires a non-empty password.

Services call object-ID endpoints such as basket, address and card with client-supplied IDs. Authorization is left to the server. The interceptor and guards (request.interceptor.ts, app.guard.ts) were not inspected, so this rating covers only the services read. Client-side checks are not an enforcement boundary.
security_controls.control: Request authentication attachment and client route gating

security_controls.assessment: Guest basket data from sessionStorage is parsed in try/catch and each item is validated (integer ProductId, positive quantity). Invalid items are dropped. This is local state only and the server must still validate.

API calls use environment.hostServer, and the architecture flows list the protocol as HTTP. Sensitive data crosses this path: credentials, TOTP tokens, passwords, and a private key via submitKey. Enforcement of TLS is deployment-dependent and was not inspected.

The reviews ('posts') and orders collections are created in-process with no authentication, schema validation, or access restriction at the data layer. The embedded engine has no login of its own, so the store depends entirely on callers for authorization and input sanitisation. Only this file was inspected; caller-side controls were not assessed here.
security_controls.control: Embedded MarsDB data store access control
security_controls.domain: Query Construction and Data Access Controls

security_controls.assessment: Socket.io server restricts CORS to a single hard-coded origin (http://localhost:4200). This limits browser cross-origin access but is hard-coded, not environment-configurable, and CORS does not authenticate clients or block non-browser clients.

The connection handler accepts any client without a token, session or handshake check, and immediately emits stored challenge notifications to it. No io.use middleware is visible in the inspected file.

Handlers take untyped data (any) with no schema validation. Any client can remove notifications by sending a matching flag, and can trigger challenge-solving logic. Some handlers use optional chaining or Array.isArray checks, but these are ad hoc. The event effects are limited to application challenge state.

The SQLite database is a plain file at data/juiceshop.sqlite. The Sequelize constructor uses placeholder credentials ('database', 'username', 'password'), which SQLite ignores, so there is no database-level authentication. The configuration shows no at-rest encryption. Protection depends on file system permissions and application-layer controls, which were not inspected here.
security_controls.control: Database storage encryption and access authentication

security_controls.assessment: The login query is built by string interpolation of req.body.email into raw SQL. This allows SQL injection and authentication bypass. The password is hashed before interpolation, but the email is not escaped or parameterized.
security_controls.domain: Query Construction and Data Access Controls

security_controls.assessment: Passwords are hashed with unsalted MD5, which is fast and vulnerable to rainbow-table and brute-force attacks. The security-answer HMAC uses a hardcoded key at line 42.

Tokens are RS256-signed with a 6h expiry, and the express-jwt middleware verifies them against the public key. However, the private key is embedded in source, so anyone with the source can forge tokens. Tokens are also kept in an in-memory map with no revocation or logout invalidation. The unverified jws.decode in the role checks is gated by verify().

Role checks for accounting, deluxe and customer verify the token signature and then check the role claim. The deluxe token is an HMAC keyed with the private key. The forgeable-key issue limits their strength.

Reset relies only on a knowledge-based security answer, compared as a keyed HMAC. The endpoint is unauthenticated. No rate limiting or lockout was observed in the inspected files, so answers can be guessed repeatedly.

Login issues a temporary token requiring a TOTP second factor when a totpSecret is set. routes/2fa.ts was not inspected, so TOTP verification was not assessed. The SQL injection in the first step can bypass the credential check.
The allowlist check uses substring matching with url.includes, so an attacker URL containing an allowed URL passes.
